titleStmt.title: Inserting DVFS Code in Hard Real-Time System Tasks

analytic.title: Inserting DVFS Code in Hard Real-Time System Tasks

application.desc: GROBID - A machine learning software for extracting information from scholarly documents

div.p: Applying Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS) in real-time systems is not a trivial task. Real-Time tasks are bounded to timing constraints in such a way that a simple performance degradation may cause the system to totally fail. Thus, this work aims at gathering two DVFS approaches (intra and inter-tasks) to define a methodology to optimize energy consumption in hard real-time systems. The intra-task approach analyzes the execution flow of a task and identifies where new instructions can be inserted in order to change supply voltage and frequency when the worst-case path is not followed. On the other hand, the inter-task analyzes how long a task waits due to interferences (e.g. preemption, shared resources), verifies system schedulability, and defines a set of initial optimal frequencies in multi-task environment. The proposed method generates a new code with the same functionality as the original one, but with the advantage of having instructions to change voltage and frequency while taking into account the task interferences, and the new added overheads. Moreover, the experimental results show that not only timing constraints were satisfied, but also that the energy consumption was reduced around 16% and 18% compared to the total consumption of the highest available frequency in two evaluated paths.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Complementary Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor (CMOS) is one of the most used technology in processor design [1]. One of its features allows, via software, the Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS) of the processor at run-time.
The energy consumption in CMOS circuits is composed of static and dynamic parts [2]. The dynamic power consumption is defined approximately as:
div.formula: E ∝ C L × N cycles × V 2
div.p: dd , where E is the dynamic energy consumption, C L is the load capacitance, N cycles is the number of processor cycles, and V dd is the supply voltage [3]. Further, the leakage in transistors is responsible for the static power consumption, which is considered constant in this paper.

Due to the quadratic dependency on supply voltage in the dynamic power equation, energy consumption can be potentially reduced when lowering the voltage. However, a reduction in supply voltage typically requires decreasing frequency, hence reducing the processor's performance.

To clarify how energy consumption can be reduced by dynamically changing supply voltage and frequency, let's assume a processor which can change frequency at run-time. This processor executes a task τ 1 , whose deadline is 100ms. If τ 1 is executed with frequency F and voltage V , its execution time T takes 50ms to finish. By comparing the execution time to the deadline, the processor stays at idle state for 50ms, in which energy consumption still occurs. Although, if we reduce both voltage and frequency by half, τ 1 deadline can still be met, because T = 50ms,

, and energy consumption is 1/4 lower [3]. DVFS has inter and intra-task as common approaches. In the inter-task, the new supply voltage values are based on the taskby-task execution analysis. The authors in [1], [4], [5] mostly try to minimize the idle time among tasks by applying a lower frequency at the beginning in order to meet their constraints and reduce energy consumption.

The intra-task approach analyzes only the execution flow of one task to compute the new voltage and frequency. Some studies [3], [6], [7] use techniques such as the worstcase execution path evaluation, code instrumentation, and task profiling, to compute the new frequency.

In hard real-time systems, the use of the DVFS technique with inter or intra-task approach is not trivial. By reducing voltage and frequency, the processor's performance is also decreased, changing the execution time of a task. Thus, this reduction must be carefully conducted, guaranteeing that timing constraints are still met.

The main contributions of this work are: (I) the combination of two DVFS approaches (inter and intra-task) in a new methodology in order to further reduce power consumption and guaranteeing the task model schedulability; (II) the use of the optimal initial set of frequencies when starting each task with a DVFS intra-task approach; (III) reducing the frequency during task execution despite of using the optimal initial set; (IV) meeting tasks' deadlines by using the response time as the new deadline of each task while keeping the task model schedulable.

In the next section, we describe our proposed methodology. Section 3 defines the setup for the test environment. The experimental results are evaluated in Section 4. Section 5 presents some related works. Finally, Section 6 concludes this paper and presents some future work.

div.head: II. PROPOSED METHODOLOGY
div.p: In the intra-task part of our methodology, we statically analyze a task, written in C99, to extract its control flow graph (c) WCEC (W.), RWCEC (R.), and SEC (S.).
W.12 W.12 W.9 W.17 and to find its worst-case execution path. Then, we are able to identify the points in which both voltage and frequency can be dynamically changed [3].

In the inter-task part of our methodology, we verify the schedulability of a task model according to the information obtained in the intra-task part, e.g. processor cycles, needed to execute the worst-case path. The inter-task also gives the optimal set of initial frequencies for the given task model whether it passed on the schedulability test [5].

By gathering information on both intra and inter-task parts, we can generate a new code, which has instructions to change voltage and frequency at run-time with the same functionality of the original one, while also considering interferences, e.g. priority and shared resources, and the new added overheads in a multi-tasks environment.

div.head: A. Control Flow Graph and Worst-Case Execution Path
div.p: We generate the Control Flow Graph (CFG), which is an abstraction of all possible execution flows of a task, in order to statically analyze the task source code. In Figures 1a and1b, we show a simple source code and its CFG, which can be defined as: (i) nodes, which means each C block (B.); (ii) edges, which are transition between blocks; (iii) conditional nodes representing an if statement, so if this node has a then and an else deviations, the CFG has a conditional nodeif, with two children -then and else; (iv) conditional nodes representing a loop statement with also two children, e.g. if there is a while statement, its condition represents the conditional node in the CFG and both inside node and the outside node as children of the conditional node; (v) subgraphs representing each C function of a task. It is worth mentioning that arbitrary control flows, e.g. goto, are not supported yet.

However, the CFG lacks some information. For instance, it is not possible to know which path is the worst one based on the previous definitions. In order to get the worst path, we can compute the cost, in processor cycles, to execute each C block and include this value as a weight of a CFG node, since it aids us to calculate the total cost of each CFG's path.

One way to compute the number of cycles needed for a C block is to partially compile this block to Assembly code. Then, based on the processor's datasheet, we can check how many processor cycles are required to run each instruction in the C block and sum their values. The result of this process is the cost to execute a node of the CFG.

To map the generated Assembly code to each high-level block, the C code can be compiled for the instruction set of the armv4t family using gcc with debug option. This option inserts the expression .loc in the translated Assembly code, which tells the line number of the C code that all Assembly instructions below .loc belong to.

The main benefit of correlating Assembly instructions to their line of the high-level code is to store the start and end lines of a block in a node of the CFG. Then, we sum the cost of all instructions of a node in order to compute its total cost, which is called Worst-Case Execution Cycles (WCEC) -illustrated as W. in Figure 1c.

It is worth mentioning that the WCEC of a loop statement is treated as a special case in our work since its number of iterations is non-deterministic. So, we rely on user annotation to estimate the total cost. For instance, in Figure 1a (line 12), user annotates the pattern "//@LOOP MAX iterations" next to the loop conditional node.

It is possible to explain some other important definitions for the CFG based on how the WCEC is calculated in our work, such as the Remaining Worst-Case Execution Cycles, the Worst-Case Execution Path, and the Saved Execution Cycles.

Remaining Worst-Case Execution Cycles (RWCEC) means how many cycles still remain to be executed until the end of the worst-case path. This definition is normally set as the edges weight of the CFG. For instance, based on the graph from Figure 1b, the edge B1 → B2 has its RWCEC (R.) equals to 159 according to the weighted graph of Figure 1c. Nevertheless, edge B2(W.12) → B3(W.9) has RW CEC = 14, that is, if the task's current flow follows the edge B2 → B3 after leaving B2, only 14 cycles remain to finish the worst path execution.

Worst-Case Execution Path (WCEP) is the worst path of a CFG, i.e., the path that leads to the highest total cost. In Figure 1c, the task's WCEC is 171 and WCEP = {B1, B2, B4, B5, B6, B5, B6, B5, B6, B5, B7} based on Figure 1b.

On the WCEP example, it is notable that {B5, B6} appear three times as they are nodes of a loop, which is executed at most three times according to user annotation. Although, the fourth time B5 occurs is due to a loop condition always be executed before breaking it.

The last definition for the CFG is the Saved Execution Cycles (SEC), which represents how many cycles were "saved" of being executed, i.e. how many cycles were not executed since the task's flow was different from the WCEP. For instance, in Figure 1b, if the deviation B2 → B4 is followed, the current path executes one edge of the WCEP seeing that RW CEC = 147. If B2 → B3 is used instead, a path different from the WCEP is followed whose RWCEC is equal to 14 cycles. Comparing both RWCECs, we can see how many cycles were not executed, or saved, due to the deviation of WCEP, SEC = RW CEC B2→B4 -RW CEC B2→B3 = 133.

Unfortunately, finding the WCEP is not a trivial task. This problem is the dual of shortest path problem in graph theory. The WCEP is derived from the Longest Path Problem, which is classified as NP-Hard. It means the WCEP problem cannot be solved in polynomial time. A negative point to the static analysis.

Although, by evaluating the unique variables of our problem: (i) the CFG is a directed graph, (ii) start and end nodes are known, and (iii) loops may exist in CFG's path, finding the WCEP may not be a problem at all.

For instance, considering a CFG with loops, in the same way we can represent functions as a subgraph, we can do it to loops. Each one of them is replaced by a single node whose WCEC is equal to each loop's worst execution in the task's paths. When identifying a loop condition node, a new node, what we call pseudo-node, is created and all parents of the condition start to point to the pseudo-node. Besides, the condition children that are not inside the loop become the children of the pseudo-node, which has a reference to loop condition. Then, by replacing all loops, the new CFG can be seen as a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG), as shown in Figure 1d.

Even though WCEP problem is NP-Hard, the complexity of finding the worst-case path is feasible by changing the CFG to a DAG. Thus, any algorithms that visit all nodes of a graph, e.g. Breadth-First Search or Depth-First Search, can be used to find the WCEP.

Therefore, the intra-task part of our methodology works as follows: we statically analyze a task source code and extract its CFG; each node of the CFG keeps the start and end lines of the block it is related to; the WCEC of a node is computed based on processor's datasheet; the CFG is transformed in a DAG; we find the WCEP after visiting the CFG's nodes and set the RWCEC of each edge.

div.head: B. WCEP Deviation and New Frequency Equations
div.p: When a deviation from the WCEP happens, an edge with SEC is defined since less cycles are executed. In our proposal, this type of edge is the best place to calculate and apply the new frequency to still meet a task's deadline.
According to Shin et al. [3], type-B and type-L are the two types of edges where DVFS technique can be applied.

Definition 1 (Type-B Edge): Given a CF G = (N, E), where N is the set of nodes and E the set of edges, u, v, w ∈ N . To (u, v), (u, w) ∈ E and assuming that u is the conditional node of an if statement, v is the then flow, w is the else flow, and R(u, v) is the RWCEC of (u, v), a type-B edge can be defined as type-B((u, v), (u, w))
div.formula: equals to (u, v) if R(u, v) ≤ R(u, w) or (u, w) if R(u, v) > R(u, w).
div.p: Considering that a static frequency was used in a target node v of (u, v) edge. If the source node u was using a greater frequency than v, then the processor energy consumption is decreased. Although, if the frequency used in u is less than v, then the energy consumption is increased.
Shin et al. [3] define a frequency update ratio to overcome static frequency problem. This ratio means how many times RW CEC(u, v) is less than RW CEC(u, w),
div.formula: for RW CEC(u, v) ≤ RW CEC(u, w). Type-B ratio is ratio B (B cond , B i ) = R(B i )/(R(succ worst (B cond )) - OHD(B)) and F new (B cond , B i ) = F cur (B cond ) × ratio B (B cond , B i ),
div.p: where ratio B (B cond , B i ) is the frequency update ratio, B cond the conditional node of a if statement, and B i , i ∈ {then, else} the target node; R(B i ) is the RWCEC of B i ; succ worst (B cond ) is the successor of B cond with the highest RWCEC; OHD(B) is the overhead of a type-B edge, i.e. it is the cost in cycles to execute a type-B analysis since new instructions must be added to the original code to calculate and change frequency, plus the number of cycles needed to make frequency and voltage transition by the processor. F cur (B cond ) is the current frequency used in B cond and F new (B cond , B i ) is the new frequency to be applied in B i .

Definition 2 (Type-L Edge): Given a CF G = (N, E), where N is the set of nodes and E the set of edges. To u, v, w ∈ N , (u, v), (v, u), (u, w) ∈ E, and assuming that u is the conditional node of a loop and L = (u, v), (v, u) the loop set of nodes, an type-L edge (u, w) is defined as type-L((u, w)) equals to 1 if (u, w) / ∈ L or 0 if (u, w) ∈ L. In other words, type-L edges are always the ones that have a node outside the loop as its target. The number of cycles that were left without execution in a loop can be calculated as:
div.formula: SEC L = W CEC(loop once )×(N worst (loop)-N exec (loop)),
div.p: where W CEC(loop once ) is the number of cycles to execute the loop once in the worst-case without the last execution of the condition node, since it is not part of each iteration; N worst (loop) is the number of iterations in the worst-case (the user input value mentioned in Section II-A); N exec (loop) is the number of loop iterations at run-time. If N exec (loop) = N worst (loop), then loop worst-case was executed.

The calculation of the frequency update ratio for type-L edges has some small differences from type-B, such as OHD(L), which means the overhead added due to type-L computation. The frequency update ratio is ratio
div.formula: L (B cond , B j ) = R(B j )/(R(B j ) + SEC L -OHD(L)) and F new (B cond , B j ) = F cur (B cond ) × ratio L (B cond , B j )
div.p: It is worth mentioning that for type-L and type-B edges the calculation of new frequency is based exclusively on the CFG information. Thus, frequency should only be changed when ratio B (B cond , B i ) < 1 or ratio L (B cond , B j ) < 1. Otherwise, due to overheads or to low value of SEC L , the frequency update ratio between nodes may not be good enough to reduce energy consumption.

div.head: C. Initial Frequency
div.p: The work of Shin et al. [3] simply cannot guarantee energy efficiency neither timing constraints when applied to multi-task environments. They can only handle mono-task environments without any task's interference. Valentin et al. [5] show how to compute the set of optimal initial frequencies for a task model based on response time schedulability analysis in order to reduce energy consumption in a multi-task environment.

Based on Valentin et al. [5], we assume a processor with DVFS support and X available frequencies. The set of possible frequencies is F = {f i | f i frequency in Hz and 1 ≤ i ≤ X}; M is a model of N tasks with fixed priority; β is the set whose elements are N-tuples, K ∈ β, with K = (f 1 , f 2 , f 3 , . . . , f n ), where f i ∈ F . K represents a possible configuration of frequencies that can be assigned to M , i.e., for
div.formula: τ i ∈ M, 1 ≤ i ≤ N , f 1 is set to τ 1 , f 2 to
div.p: τ 2 and so on.

As K ∈ β, β holds all frequency combinations to run model M . Furthermore, there are X N possible combinations, an exponential problem which Valentin et al. proposed an heuristic algorithm to get the response in a reasonable time.

In the context of hard real-time systems, K is only feasible if M passes in the schedulability ∀i < N, R i (K) ≤ D i , where R i (K) is τ i response time in function of K, and D i the deadline of τ i .

The response time is also defined as: R i (K) = I i (K) + J i . I i (K) is the time a task τ i was not executed with one of the frequencies of K due to the interferences of other tasks, e.g. task preemption; and J i is the worst time to release a task for execution, i.e. it is the release jitter of τ i .

Considering C i (f ) as the computing time of τ i in function of f : C i (f ) = W CEC(τ i ) / f, the interferences in τ i in function of K related to the maximum time it may be blocked (B i ), can be computed as defined in Equation ( 1). The interested reader can found more details in Valentin et al. [5].

div.p: Then, the optimal initial frequencies set is the one which minimizes the energy in M . It is defined as The process of identifying type-B and type-L edges, and inserting instructions to change voltage and frequency, define the new code generation. The major gain of this step is to help developers to automatically analyze a task flow and to make a code with energy optimization instructions.

div.head: E. Methodology Definition
div.p: Figure 3 shows our proposed methodology. First, the CFG + WCEP step statically analyzes the behavior of each task of a given task model in order to construct the CFGs. Then, the cost of each node in the CFG is computed by translating C code into Assembly. After that, the CFG is simplified to a DAG, allowing the computation of the WCEP.

On Schedulability Information I, the task model pass through the schedulability test. This first test aims to verify whether the task model given is schedulable as it is. If the test fails, our methodology cannot be applied. Otherwise, we take the set of optimal initial frequencies to start the task model.

In the next step, WCEP Deviation and Code Generation, type-B and type-L edges are identified, and using the start lines of CFG nodes, we can generate a new code with the same functionality of the original one, but now supporting changing frequency dynamically.

When computing a new frequency value, Shin et al. [3] guarantee that, a task finishes its execution before or at the same time of its deadline in a mono-task environment. However, in a multi-task environment, the authors cannot assure whether the deadline will be missed, because they do not take into account interferences in a task, even if the task model starts all tasks with the optimal frequencies set.

According to Valentin et al. [5], by using schedulability test in a task model, we can compute not only the optimal initial frequencies set, but also the response time of each task. This time means that, in order for the task model to be still schedulable, each task must finish its execution until the response time, which is less or equal to the deadline.

Even though our intra-task part makes a task finishes as far as its deadline, the task model may not be schedulable in a multi-task environment. If, instead of using the original deadline, we define the task response time as the new deadline, the frequency update ratio is computed based on the response time. So, by finishing each task in its new deadline, the schedulability test must succeed.

It is worth mentioning that whenever a type-B or type-L edge happens, new instructions are always inserted. Although, type-L edges are the only ones which can be presented in WCEP, because these edges are not a truly deviation. If a loop executes less iterations than its maximum, it passes by a type-L edge in the same way it should when executing all iterations, no matter whether it is in the WCEP or not. In this way, the overhead of a type-L edge can be added to a task WCEC.

By changing the WCEC values, the test done in Schedulability Information I may not still be true. That is the main reason why step Schedulability Information II is needed. We check whether, after adding overheads to the tasks WCECs and using their response time as the new deadline, the task model passes the schedulability test again. As a result, we can have not only a new set of optimal initial frequencies, which may be greater than the previous one, but also new response times that replace previous deadlines.

The four steps described in this section define our methodology and how it works to optimize energy consumption of a given task model in a multi-task environment. More details about our proposal implementation is available in cfg -Control Flow Graph of C File1 .

div.head: III. EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
div.p: In this section, we describe our experimental environment. We compare energy consumption of our proposed model to (i) the use of the highest frequency in the system, and (ii) the work in Valentin et al. [5]. Even though we also based our methodology on Shin et al. [3], it is not used for comparison since it is not suitable for multi-task environment neither considers tasks interferences.

In our test environment, we are simulating the execution of CFG by a processor. There is no real processor being used since we built a tool to walk through the paths of a CFG and consuming its cycles such as a processor. Moreover, we are not taking into account memory, pipeline, energy consumption in idle time, or any architectural overheads in our experimental environment. However, we are computing the overheads caused by the calculation of frequency update ratio when following type-B or type-L edges, and the one due to voltage and frequency transition. For instance, the overhead of underclocking phenomenon in which processor operates at a higher voltage than what is strictly necessary, while voltage is changing to a lower level [8].

In this paper, we are considering the upper bound overhead of 20.000 cycles used by Shin et al. [3] to execute type-B or type-L instructions and change voltage and frequency. The energy spent by one overhead is related to the voltage used when checking whether the changing was possible. Also, we are considering that every time a voltage transition happens, processor halts until the changing is done.
We define three paths to properly execute a CFG: the worst, middle, and approximated best path.

By definition, assuming a set P of all CFG paths and N tasks: P = {p i | ec(p 1 ) < ec(p 2 ) < . . . < ec(p n )}, where ec(p i ) is the number of cycles needed to execute path p i . Strictly speaking, P is the set of all CFG paths ordered by the cost in cycles of each path. In this way, the worst path is defined as p n , which is the path in P with the highest cost. Additionally, W CEC = ec(p n ) is the task WCEC.

Still, the middle path is defined as: p m = P (1+len(P )/2), where len(P ) is the size of P -the number of paths in CFG. p m is the median path in P . If len(P ) is odd, p m is the middle element. If len(P ) is even, P is divided in two parts, then we take the last element of the first part -p k , and the first element of the second part -p z . The middle path p m is p z , since ec(p z ) > ec(p k ).

The approximated best path is the last evaluated path. The choice of this path happened due to the fact that the CFG best path has a really low cost, which could not be used to measure frequency changes. The approximated best path is For instance, assuming the WCECs used by Valentin was the same of Proposal, the energy consumption is not less than Valentin's by the end of tasks execution, because the set of initial frequencies is different from Valentin, which used the optimal one for its given task model.

Even though Proposal energy consumption was greater than Valentin's, it was not compared to Worst-Case. However, considering a task model in which the processor has few cycles to execute, the WCEP of each task has overheads due to type-B and type-L edges instructions, and the schedulability may be only possible if Proposal operates with the highest available frequency, so the energy consumption of Proposal may surely be greater than Valentin's and Worst-Case.

Middle Path: by following a path different from Worst Path, deviations in a task CFG happens and type-B and type-L edges are found. In this case, frequency may change according to each execution context.

Figure 5 shows the total energy consumption of each method when the Middle Path is followed and frequency changes. As we can see, Worst-Case spent more energy than Proposal, which had 18% of energy reduction while Valentin had 10%.

According to Tables II andIII, the Middle Path WCEC on Proposal is higher than the other methods, i.e. the overheads are a result of type-B and type-L edges. The set of initial frequencies is also different from the one used by Valentin. Contrasting the Worst Path, frequency was not only changed, but it also made energy consumption be less than Valentin's during Proposal execution.

The energy reduction in Middle Path was only possible because of Proposal's intra-task part where frequency changes at run-time when a path deviates from Worst Path. Still, following a type-B or type-L edge does not mean frequency changes, it is only allowed whether the ratio is less than one according to each edge type.

Approximated Best Path: Once again, Worst-Case had the highest total energy consumption, while Valentin was higher than Proposal in Figure 6, i.e. 10% of energy reduction of Valentin compared to 16% of Proposal. The Approximated Best Path, similar to the other two paths and according to Tables II andIII, has the WCEC values and the set of initial frequencies of Proposal greater than Worst-Case and Valentin. Although, frequency was changed at runtime as a result of type-B and type-L edges. The change made lower frequencies to be used in order to reduce energy consumption, which gave Proposal better results than the other methods.

From the three analyzed cases, some main notes need to be pointed out. (i) Having type-B or type-L edges in a given path is not a synonym of frequency changes, (ii) neither the change always makes the energy reduction be less than before.

Considering that frequency has changed to a lower value at run-time when a path deviates from WCEP, the energy consumption at this point is less indeed. Fewer instructions are executed per second, voltage is reduced, and energy consumption also decreases. On the other hand, overheads due to new instructions and DVFS transitions were added, so, before starting consuming less energy, the one spent by the overheads must be equalized.

For instance, a CFG is being executed and, before its last node, we follow a type-B edge where frequency can be changed to a lower value. The point is, considering 100 cycles as the cost of the last node, the overhead of type-B edge plus DVFS transition may be higher than the energy spent by the new frequency when executing those cycles. In this case, even though frequency has changed, the total energy consumption is greater than before when frequency was not changed.

Hence, in our experimental environment on tasks with high WCECs, when Proposal changed frequency, lower values were not only applied, but also energy consumption was reduced for Middle and Approximated Best Path. However, the Worst Path showed how overheads play a critical role in our methodology.

V. RELATED WORK Shin et al. [3] perform a static program-analysis to extract the WCEP in order to identify type-B and type-L edges, where DVFS may be applied. Azevedo et al. [7] apply the DVFS based on task profiling. However, the authors and Shin et al. [3] have a common problem, they use the ideal frequency. In other words, they use it as a continuous value instead of the discrete ones available in the processor. Another difference from our proposal is that both works do not handle multi-task environments.

On the other hand, Kim et al. [4] propose an algorithm to estimate idle time of real-time periodic tasks under Earliest Deadline First (EDF) scheduling. Our proposal not only works in multi-task environment, but also does not depend on EDF.

Tatematsu et al. [6] show a study based on task execution profiling. The authors identify checkpoints where DVFS can be applied. However, they can miss task's deadline since they did not define how many checkpoints should be used.

Pan et al. [10] propose an algorithm for energy saving considering soft real-time tasks with stochastic execution times in a mono-processor. Even though the authors reach an approximated optimal solution, they are assuming independent and non-preemptive tasks, and do not take into account possible frequency changes.

Ghor et al. [11] adopts DVFS in real-time tasks to show how to decrease the deadline miss ratio in a mono-processor and energy harvesting system -where its supply energy is draw from the environment. However, the authors do not consider both (i) the frequency switching energy overhead, and (ii) the running frequency reduction due to intra-DVFS.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
div.p: In this paper, we proposed a methodology to take a code from a hard real-time task, with no energy efficiency information, and transform it into a new one, with energy-related instructions inserted, where supply and frequency can be dynamically changed, in a multi-task environment. Besides the addition of new instructions, the functionality of the original code is still the same and its timing requirements are met.

The combination of inter and intra-task approaches for code generation with DVFS technique, showed that energy consumption can be reduced even with the use of optimal initial frequencies. To achieve this goal, we statically analyze a task's flow to find places (type-B and type-L edges) where instructions to change frequency may be inserted. Moreover, our proposal verifies if our changes still make the task model schedulable due to the addition of overheads. So, in a path different from the WCEP, we can have less energy spent depending on the given task model.

It is worth mentioning that "80% of a task execution runs in 20% of its code" [12], the called Pareto Principle, which is also known as the 80-20 rule. As long as our best results were in Middle and Approximated Best Path, as future work, we intend to find the most common paths of a task CFG and verify if the overheads can be reduced by only using DVFS technique in those paths. In this way, not only overheads may be minimized due to the new code, but also the ones from DVFS transitions. We also plan to add other architectural overheads in future analyzes.

The 15% number was used based on empirical tests of our tasks benchmarks showing that the frequency changes could be properly measured.

In Gustafsson et al. [9], the authors define a set of tasks that are independent from any system or third party libraries, i.e. all auxiliary functions are implemented in the same C file. Then, we chose eight tasks written in C99 and change them to have all of its execution limited to the main function due to our parser tool limitation, which is not handling more than one function in a file yet. Table I shows the used task model.

The supply voltages and frequencies used by our simulation environment were taken from a Intel XScale, however the processor itself wast not used since our simulation tool acts as a processor. The frequencies and voltages are 1000MHz -1.8V, 800MHz -1.6V, 600MHz -1.3V, 400MHz -1.0V, and 150MHz -0.75V.

Our simulation end time is equal to the task model hyperperiod, i.e. the end time is equal to the least common multiple (LCM) of all periods in Table I, 504,000 milliseconds. Then, all tasks must be finished with their own deadlines met at the hyperperiod.

We used the following abbreviations to simplify the results explanations: Worst-Case, the use of the highest frequency available, 1000MHz; Valentin, always referring to [5]; Proposal, our inter and intra-task methodology; Frequency Changes, always means changing "voltage and frequency" at run-time.

In this section we defined the main points of our experimental environment: (i) a simulation tool 3 to act as processor executing a CFG's path; (ii) the end time of the task model as the LCM of the periods; (iii) the overheads as the execution of type-B or type-L edges and frequency transition; (iv) the worst, middle, and approximated best paths to execute in each task; (v) a total of eight tasks as part of the task model; (vi) the frequencies and voltages to be used.

div.head: IV. PERFORMANCE EVALUATION
div.p: First of all, the task model used in our experimental environment is subject to Deadline Monotonic scheduling, which means the lower the task deadline in Table I, the higher its 3 Simulation tool on https://github.com/diegoValhalla/cfg-wcec-sim priority. Additionally, preemption is the only interference used in task model.

Based on the WCEP, we started using Valentin to check system schedulability. This step gives the set of optimal initial frequencies, the response time of each task, and the cost of each path used by Valentin and Worst-Case. All these information is showed in Table II.

As long as the task model is schedulable, we applied our Proposal and identified type-B and type-L edges. Then, the instructions to compute the frequency update ratio and change frequency were added, and the new code of each task was generated. However, all the changes to the previous code added overheads which can make the task model not schedulable anymore (see the WCEC value of 'Worst' column in Table III).

After checking system schedulability with the new task model, the system was still schedulable. The set of initial frequency and response times, on the other hand, have changed. These new values in Table III are used by Proposal, because it was not fair to make Worst-Case and Valentin execute a code with overheads that they do not use.
In what follows, we first analyze the Worst Path and how overheads can negatively increase energy consumption. After that, our analysis goes to the Middle and Approximated Best Path.
Worst Path: by first analyzing the data in Tables II andIII, we can see that, due to overheads in the WCEP, the tasks' WCEC used by Proposal are greater than the ones in Worst-Case and Valentin.

With more cycles to consume in the Worst Path and a different set of initial frequencies, energy consumption on Proposal may be higher than Valentin's, because the frequencies in Table II is already the optimal one. Thus, any set different from that spent more energy, and, since we are following the Worst Path, our intra-task part cannot be applied to change frequency.

In Figure 4, the total energy spent by Proposal was indeed higher than Valentin's when comparing both energy consumptions to Worst-Case. Proposal had 7% of energy reduction against 10% from Valentin. This was expected since Proposal has more cycles to execute and the set of initial frequencies is different from Valentin, but not all the set frequencies are equal to the highest one.
